q: Which Gaudí building has an undulating stone façade?
n: Casa Milà has an undulating stone facade, which earned it the quarry nickname. Source: UNESCO (Works of Antoni Gaudí).

q: Which Gaudí project began as a private housing estate and is now a public park in Barcelona?
n: Park Güell began as a private garden-city housing estate for Eusebi Güell and is now a public park in Barcelona. Source: UNESCO (Works of Antoni Gaudí); Park Güell official site.

q: What iconic feature is at the entrance of Park Güell?
n: The entrance stairway of Park Güell features the mosaic dragon (salamander), "El Drac". Source: Park Güell official site.

q: Which is one of Frank Lloyd Wright's most iconic works of organic architecture?
n: Fallingwater (1935–39) is one of Frank Lloyd Wright's most iconic works of organic architecture. Source: Western Pennsylvania Conservancy; UNESCO.

q: Which ambitious Frank Lloyd Wright tower was never built?
n: Wright's Mile High Illinois (1956), a mile-tall skyscraper, was never built. Source: Frank Lloyd Wright Foundation.

q: Who coined "form follows function"?
n: Louis Sullivan coined "form follows function" in his 1896 essay "The Tall Office Building Artistically Considered". Source: Sullivan (1896); Encyclopaedia Britannica.

q: Which Frank Lloyd Wright house has cantilevered terraces over a waterfall?
n: Fallingwater (the Kaufmann house) has cantilevered concrete terraces over the waterfall at Bear Run. Source: Western Pennsylvania Conservancy.

q: Which Wright project in Arizona was both a school and his winter home?
n: Taliesin West in Scottsdale, Arizona (from 1937) was Wright's winter home and school. Source: Frank Lloyd Wright Foundation; UNESCO.

q: Mies designed the Farnsworth House. Who designed The Glass House?
n: Philip Johnson designed The Glass House in New Canaan, Connecticut (1949). Source: The Glass House (National Trust) official site.

q: Who coined the term "International Style," with Henry-Russell Hitchcock?
n: Philip Johnson coined "International Style" with Henry-Russell Hitchcock for the 1932 MoMA exhibition and book. Source: MoMA archives; Encyclopaedia Britannica.

q: Who was the architect of The Glass House and the first recipient of the Pritzker Architecture Prize?
n: Philip Johnson built The Glass House (1949) and was the first Pritzker Prize laureate (1979). Source: Pritzker Architecture Prize.

q: Who collaborated with Mies van der Rohe on the Seagram Building?
n: Philip Johnson collaborated with Mies van der Rohe on the Seagram Building (1958), designing interiors including the Four Seasons restaurant. Source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Seagram Building.

q: When was Philip Johnson's Glass House built?
n: Philip Johnson's Glass House was completed in 1949. The house is a single glass-walled room on a brick base, set in a landscaped estate in New Canaan, Connecticut. Source: The Glass House official site.

q: What was Norman Foster's first high-rise on Hong Kong Island?
n: Norman Foster's first high-rise on Hong Kong Island was the HSBC Main Building (1985). Source: Foster + Partners project page.

q: Which modernist master, interested in modular building and minimalism, is famous for tubular-steel furniture?
n: Marcel Breuer is famous for tubular-steel furniture such as the Wassily chair, and for interest in modular, minimal building. Source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Marcel Breuer.

q: Who designed the geodesic dome for Expo 67 in Montreal?
n: R. Buckminster Fuller designed the geodesic dome US Pavilion for Expo 67 in Montreal (now the Biosphère). Source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Buckminster Fuller.

q: Which German architect founded the Bauhaus?
n: Walter Gropius founded the Bauhaus in Weimar in 1919. The Bauhaus later moved to Dessau (1925) and Berlin, and was closed under Nazi pressure in 1933. Source: UNESCO (Bauhaus and its Sites).

q: Which Brazilian architect is best known for free-form curves and sculptural modernism?
n: Oscar Niemeyer of Brazil is best known for free-form curves and sculptural modernism, as in Brasília. Source: Pritzker Architecture Prize (1988); UNESCO (Brasília).

q: Who designed the glass pyramid at the Louvre?
n: I.M. Pei designed the glass pyramid at the Louvre (1989). Source: Louvre official site; Pritzker Prize (1983).

q: Who designed Dulles International Airport and the St. Louis Gateway Arch?
n: Eero Saarinen designed both Dulles International Airport and the St. Louis Gateway Arch. Source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Eero Saarinen.

q: Who is best known for the Twin Towers of the World Trade Center?
n: Minoru Yamasaki is best known for the Twin Towers of the World Trade Center (1973). Source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Minoru Yamasaki.

q: Who designed the Auditorio de Tenerife "Adán Martín"?
n: The Auditorio de Tenerife "Adán Martín" (2003) was designed by Santiago Calatrava. Source: Auditorio de Tenerife official site.

q: What was Le Corbusier's real name?
n: Le Corbusier's real name was Charles-Édouard Jeanneret-Gris. He was born in La Chaux-de-Fonds, Switzerland. Source: Fondation Le Corbusier.

q: Which architect, designer, painter, planner and writer, a pioneer of modern architecture, designed the Villa Savoye?
n: Le Corbusier, architect, designer, painter, planner and writer, designed the Villa Savoye. Source: Fondation Le Corbusier; UNESCO.

q: When was the Villa Savoye built?
n: The Villa Savoye in Poissy was designed in 1928 and completed in 1931. It is Le Corbusier's clearest demonstration of his Five Points of a New Architecture (pilotis, free plan, free facade, ribbon windows, roof garden). Source: Fondation Le Corbusier; UNESCO (The Architectural Work of Le Corbusier).

q: During the 1920s, Le Corbusier was known for promoting this Architectural Style.
n: In the 1920s Le Corbusier's Purist villas (Villa Stein, Villa Savoye) were smooth, white, cubic volumes, a "white box" modernism that the 1932 MoMA show grouped into the International Style. Brutalism came later with his béton brut work. Source: Curtis, Modern Architecture Since 1900; Fondation Le Corbusier.

q: Who designed Notre-Dame-du-Haut at Ronchamp, France?
n: Notre-Dame-du-Haut at Ronchamp (1950–55) is Le Corbusier's sculptural pilgrimage chapel, with a curved concrete roof and deep-set coloured windows. Source: UNESCO (The Architectural Work of Le Corbusier); Fondation Le Corbusier.

q: Which leading Japanese architect co-founded the Metabolist movement?
n: Kisho Kurokawa co-founded the Metabolist movement with Kiyonori Kikutake, Fumihiko Maki and others at the 1960 World Design Conference in Tokyo. His Nakagin Capsule Tower (1972) is its icon. Source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Kisho Kurokawa; Koolhaas & Obrist, Project Japan.

q: Which Japanese architect blended tradition with modernism and built on five continents?
n: Kenzo Tange fused Japanese tradition with modernism (Yoyogi National Gymnasium, Hiroshima Peace Center) and built on five continents. He won the Pritzker Prize in 1987. Source: Pritzker Architecture Prize (1987 laureate).

q: Who designed the Beijing National Stadium ("Bird's Nest")?
n: The Beijing National Stadium ("Bird's Nest") for the 2008 Olympics was designed by Herzog & de Meuron with artist Ai Weiwei and engineers Arup. Source: Herzog & de Meuron project page; Arup.

q: Which Japanese architect designed the Sendai Mediatheque?
n: Toyo Ito designed the Sendai Mediatheque (2001), with thirteen lattice steel "tubes" carrying thin floor plates. Source: Toyo Ito & Associates; Pritzker Prize (2013).

q: Which Japanese architect is known for minimalist concrete and natural light, as in the Church of the Light?
n: Tadao Ando is known for smooth exposed concrete, simple geometry and natural light. His Church of the Light (Ibaraki, Osaka, 1989) has a cross-shaped slit in the altar wall. Source: Pritzker Architecture Prize (1995 laureate); Encyclopaedia Britannica, Tadao Ando.

q: Who received the first Pritzker Architecture Prize in 1979?
n: Philip Johnson received the first Pritzker Architecture Prize in 1979. Source: Pritzker Architecture Prize (laureates list).

q: When did Kenzo Tange receive the Pritzker Prize?
n: Kenzo Tange won the Pritzker Prize in 1987, the first Japanese laureate. Source: Pritzker Architecture Prize (laureates list).

q: Who won the Pritzker Prize in 1983?
n: I.M. Pei won the 1983 Pritzker Prize and used the $100,000 award to fund a scholarship for Chinese students to study architecture in the US. Source: Pritzker Architecture Prize (1983 laureate).

q: Who won the Pritzker Prize in 2013?
n: Toyo Ito won the 2013 Pritzker Prize. Wang Shu won in 2012 and Peter Zumthor in 2009. Source: Pritzker Architecture Prize (laureates list).
